overview:
Navpad Oli, also known as Ayambil Oli or Navpada Āyambila Oli, is a major Jain observance centered on the worship and contemplation of nine supreme entities (navapada) arranged in the sacred Siddhachakra. It is regarded in many communities as one of the most important Jain festivals or parvas and is observed twice a year, in the bright fortnights (śukla pakṣa) of the lunar months of Caitra (March–April) and Āśvina/Aso (September–October). Each observance lasts nine days, traditionally from the seventh lunar day (saptamī) to the full moon (pūrṇimā). During these nine days, practitioners undertake the austerity called ayambil—eating only once a day, usually a simple, boiled, tasteless meal without oil, ghee, milk, curd, sugar, or spices—and devote each day to one of the nine pads: Arihant, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu/Sādhvī, Samyak Darśana (right faith), Samyak Jñāna (right knowledge), Samyak Cāritra (right conduct), and Samyak Tapa (right austerity).

The theological basis of Navpad Oli lies in the broader Jain reverence for the Navapada, which are also invoked in the Navkār Mantra and represented diagrammatically in the Siddhachakra yantra. The first five pads are the Pañca Parameṣṭhī—the five supreme beings who are the focus of Jain worship: Arihant (omniscient, embodied Tīrthaṅkara), Siddha (liberated, bodiless soul), Ācārya (head of the monastic order), Upādhyāya (scripture-teacher), and Sādhu/Sādhvī (monk or nun). The remaining four pads are dharma-tattvas—fundamental qualities of the path: right faith, right knowledge, right conduct, and right austerity. Together they form the core of Jain soteriology: the beings who embody liberation and the qualities that lead the practitioner toward it.

Ritually, Navpad Oli is closely associated with the Siddhachakra, a yantra or diagram in which the nine pads are arranged in a specific pattern, often with Arihant in the center and Siddha at the top, surrounded by the other beings and virtues. Devotees perform Siddhachakra pūjā, offer colored rice (vakshep), circumambulate, and recite the Navkār Mantra and other hymns that enumerate the virtues of each pad. Each day’s worship is linked to a color and to a set of guṇas (qualities) of the respective entity; for example, Arihant is often associated with white and with the destruction of inner enemies such as attachment and aversion, while Siddha is linked with red and the state of motionless, liberated existence. The ayambil fast is not merely dietary restriction but a deliberate training of the senses: by renouncing taste and culinary pleasure, the practitioner aims to weaken rāga (attachment) and dveṣa (aversion), cultivate equanimity, and focus the mind on the nine ideals.

From a doctrinal perspective, Navpad Oli reinforces the central Jain triad of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct (samyak darśana, jñāna, cāritra), often expanded to include right austerity (tapa) as a practical means of purifying karma. The nine days become a structured retreat in which laypeople approximate monastic discipline: waking early, performing pratikramaṇa (ritual repentance), engaging in kāyotsarga (standing meditation), listening to discourses, visiting temples, and practicing self-restraint in speech, movement, and consumption. Many ritual manuals prescribe detailed sequences of worship, including multiple devavandans (obeisance to deities), snātra pūjā (ritual bathing of the Jina image), aṣṭaprakārī pūjā (eightfold worship), ārati, maṅgal dīpa, and repeated recitation of Navkār-vālīs (series of Navkār Mantra repetitions dedicated to each pad).

Historically and narratively, Navpad Oli is often linked to the story of Śrīpāl and Maynā (Śrīpāl-Maynā kathā), a popular Jain narrative in which the observance of Navpad Oli and devotion to the Siddhachakra are said to bring about the cure of disease, removal of obstacles, and spiritual uplift. In this story, Śrīpāl, afflicted with leprosy, and his devoted wife Maynā undertake the Navpad Oli austerity and worship the Siddhachakra with great faith, eventually gaining both physical healing and spiritual merit. While the story is hagiographical and didactic rather than doctrinally prescriptive, it has shaped the devotional imagination around Navpad Oli, emphasizing themes of steadfast faith, the transformative power of austerity, and the compassionate grace of the Tīrthaṅkaras.

In contemporary practice, Navpad Oli is observed across Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities with regional variations in ritual detail, but the core elements remain: twice-yearly nine-day ayambil, worship of the nine pads, and focus on inner purification. Community organizations, youth groups, and temples often provide structured programs, discourses, and collective ayambil meals. Modern expositions stress that the primary aim is spiritual self-cultivation—reducing passions, reflecting on one’s conduct over the previous six months, and renewing commitment to ahiṃsā (non-violence), anekāntavāda (non-absolutism), and aparigraha (non-possessiveness). While many narratives speak of worldly benefits, traditional teachers emphasize that the true fruit of Navpad Oli is the gradual shedding of karmic bondage and the strengthening of the path toward liberation.

It is important to note that, like all Jain austerities, Navpad Oli is traditionally undertaken with attention to one’s health, capacity, and guidance from knowledgeable lay leaders or monastics. The ayambil fast is demanding, and classical manuals often describe graded observances and allowances. Any decision about prolonged fasting, especially for those with medical conditions, children, pregnant individuals, or the elderly, should be made with appropriate medical and pastoral guidance. Within Jain ethics, the intention of tapas is self-purification, not self-harm, and the observance of Navpad Oli is meant to be a disciplined yet balanced practice integrated into a life of non-violence and care.

primary_sources.title: Navkār Mantra (Namaskāra Mantra)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the Jain canonical tradition; specific authorship not ascribed
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरिहंताणं
णमो सिद्धाणं
णमो आयरियाणं
णमो उवज्झायाणं
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं

एसो पंच नमोकारो
सव्वपावप्पणासणो
मंगलाणं च सव्वेसिं
पढमं हवई मंगलं
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ
ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ
ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ
ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ
ṇamo loe savva-sāhūṇaṃ

eso paṃca namokāro
savva-pāva-ppaṇāsano
maṃgalāṇaṃ ca savvesiṃ
paḍhamaṃ havaī maṃgalaṃ
primary_sources.translation:
Obeisance to the Arihants.
Obeisance to the Siddhas.
Obeisance to the Ācāryas.
Obeisance to the Upādhyāyas.
Obeisance to all the Sādhus in the world.

This fivefold obeisance
destroys all sins
and among all auspicious things
is indeed the foremost auspiciousness.
primary_sources.notes: The Navkār Mantra is the foundational Jain prayer, found in various canonical and liturgical sources in Prakrit. It directly names the first five pads of Navpad Oli—the Pañca Parameṣṭhī—and implicitly grounds the practice of venerating these beings. Later tradition extends the scope of reverence to include the dharma-tattvas of right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity, forming the full Navapada. While the mantra itself does not describe Navpad Oli as a festival, it is the primary textual basis for the hierarchy of beings and virtues that Navpad Oli ritualizes.

primary_sources.title: Siddhachakra-stavana and related hymns
primary_sources.author: Various Jain authors; often anonymous or attributed within sectarian hymnals
primary_sources.original_text:
Sample verse (illustrative, not exhaustive):
सिद्धचक्रं नमामि जिनवराणां
नवपदं पुण्यफलप्रदं च
आरिहन्त-सिद्ध-गुरु-उपाध्याय-साधु
सम्यग्दर्शन-ज्ञान-चरित्र-तपः पदम्
primary_sources.transliteration:
siddhacakraṃ namāmi jin-varāṇāṃ
navapadaṃ puṇya-phalapradaṃ ca
ārihanta-siddha-guru-upādhyāya-sādhu
samyag-darśana-jñāna-caritra-tapaḥ padam
primary_sources.translation:
I bow to the Siddhachakra of the supreme Jinas,
to the Navapada that bestows the fruit of merit:
Arihant, Siddha, Guru (Ācārya), Upādhyāya, Sādhu,
and the pads of right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity.
primary_sources.notes: Siddhachakra-stavana texts, in Sanskrit, Prakrit, or vernaculars, praise the Siddhachakra diagram and enumerate the nine pads. They are recited during Navpad Oli and Siddhachakra pūjā. Exact wording varies by lineage and hymnal; the sample verse here is representative rather than a fixed canonical line. These hymns belong to liturgical literature (corpus tier B–D) rather than the earliest canonical strata but are central to the ritual framing of Navpad Oli.

primary_sources.title: Śrīpāl-Maynā Kathā (Story of Śrīpāl and Maynā)
primary_sources.author: Medieval Jain narrative tradition; versions exist in Prakrit, Sanskrit, and Gujarati, authorship varies
primary_sources.original_text:
Illustrative Gujarati opening (not a critical edition line):
શ્રીપાળ અને મૈના ની કથા સાંભળો ભક્તો,
નવપદ ઓળી ના મહિમા થી રોગ નિવારે છે.
primary_sources.transliteration:
śrīpāḷ ane mainā nī kathā sāṃbhaḷo bhakto,
navapada oḷī nā mahimā thī roga nivāre che.
primary_sources.translation:
Listen, devotees, to the story of Śrīpāl and Maynā;
by the glory of Navpad Oli, disease is removed.
primary_sources.notes: The Śrīpāl-Maynā story is a popular Jain narrative used in sermons and festival booklets to illustrate the power of Navpad Oli and Siddhachakra worship. Different sects and regions preserve distinct recensions. It is not a canonical āgama but belongs to narrative and didactic literature (corpus tier C–D). The story emphasizes faith, perseverance, and the spiritual benefits of Navpad Oli, but its miraculous elements are interpreted symbolically by many teachers, as encouragement toward inner transformation rather than a literal guarantee of physical cures.

primary_sources.title: Navpad Oli Vidhi (ritual manuals)
primary_sources.author: Modern ritual compilers, e.g., Yogesh Shah; various publishers
primary_sources.original_text:
Example procedural line (paraphrased from ritual manuals):
"चैत्र और आश्विन शुक्ल पक्ष की सप्तमी से पूर्णिमा तक नवपद ओली में प्रतिदिन आयम्बिल का पालन करें और सिद्धचक्र की पूजा करें।"
primary_sources.transliteration: caitra aur āśvin śukla pakṣ kī saptamī se pūrṇimā tak navapada olī meṃ pratidin āyambila kā pālana kareṃ aur siddhacakra kī pūjā kareṃ.
primary_sources.translation: From the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and Āśvin until the full moon, observe ayambil each day during Navpad Oli and perform worship of the Siddhachakra.
primary_sources.notes: Navpad Oli Vidhi texts are practical guides detailing dates, vows, and sequences of worship. They draw on older liturgical traditions and local customs. They are not primary doctrinal sources but are important for understanding how Navpad Oli is actually practiced in contemporary communities. Because they are prescriptive, they should be followed with consideration of one’s health and in consultation with knowledgeable leaders.

misconceptions.myth: Navpad Oli is only about earning worldly benefits such as health, wealth, or success, and the story of Śrīpāl and Maynā guarantees that anyone who performs the nine-day fast will be cured of illness.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional Jain teaching presents Navpad Oli primarily as a practice of inner purification, reduction of passions, and cultivation of right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity. Narrative texts like the Śrīpāl-Maynā kathā use miraculous motifs to inspire faith, but they are not doctrinal promises of automatic physical healing. Responsible observance of Navpad Oli includes attention to health, capacity, and non-violence toward oneself, and any medical concerns should be addressed with qualified healthcare professionals alongside spiritual guidance.

misconceptions.myth: Navpad Oli is a sect-specific or optional modern invention with no connection to core Jain doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: While the detailed ritual forms of Navpad Oli and Siddhachakra worship developed historically and vary by sect and region, the nine pads themselves—five supreme beings and four dharma-tattvas—are deeply rooted in core Jain doctrine, especially the Navkār Mantra and the triad of right faith, knowledge, and conduct. Navpad Oli is a ritual elaboration of these doctrinal foundations, not a disconnected innovation, though participation and specific practices remain a matter of personal vow and community custom rather than universal obligation.

misconceptions.myth: Everyone, regardless of age or health, is religiously required to perform the full nine-day ayambil fast twice a year, and reducing or modifying the fast is a sign of weak faith.
misconceptions.reality: Jain ethics emphasize non-violence, including toward one’s own body, and recognize graded vows and practices according to individual capacity. Classical and modern teachers allow for variations in fasting, such as partial ayambil, reduced days, or alternative forms of tapas, especially for children, the elderly, pregnant individuals, or those with medical conditions. Faith is expressed through sincere effort and ethical living, not through harmful extremity, and decisions about fasting should be made with both spiritual and medical counsel.
